title: Bridging-driven condensation by eukaryotic SMC complexes is a conserved feature of genome organization.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Read the open-access full text and the PubMed Central full-text XML (PMC13539107). The data availability statement says only 'All data are available in the main text or the supplementary materials' - nothing is deposited. The XML lists exactly one supplementary artefact, gkag850_supplemental_files.zip, 55,571,719 bytes (55.6 MB), declared as a zip of supplemental figures and movies; the text references Supplementary Figures S1-S10 and Movies S1-S8 and zero supplementary tables. I tried to retrieve that zip twice through the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint (killed at 75 s both times) and once through the PubMed Central /bin/ path, which returned a 1,816-byte HTML block page rather than the file; it is also over the project's 50 MB download cap. I confirmed by NCBI E-utilities that the one accession in the paper, GSE151553, is a third-party budding-yeast Micro-C (a high-resolution chromosome-contact assay) series from a 2020 paper by other authors, reused here.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All numbers: 539 +/- 65 cohesin condensates per cell from n = 7 cells, n = 8 cells imaged by super-resolution microscopy, and 1,331 / 78 / 2,721 loops from 432 / 51 / 348 parent chromatin domains in wild-type, mcd1-depleted and wpl1-depleted yeast. Also from text only: the single-molecule fluorescence movies, atomic force microscopy images, and fluorescence-recovery-after-photobleaching curves exist solely as figures and movies, and the reused public datasets are the human HFFc6 Micro-C (4D Nucleome accession 4DNFI9FVHJZQ), yeast Micro-C (GSE151553) and GM12878 RAD21 ChIP-seq.

a1_downloadable.note: The paper deposits no dataset at all: the data availability statement points to 'the main text or the supplementary materials', and the only supplementary item in the PubMed Central XML is one 55.6 MB zip of figures and movies. I could not retrieve it (Europe PMC endpoint timed out twice; PubMed Central /bin/ returned a block page) and it exceeds the 50 MB cap. No raw images, no measurement tables, no code are available anywhere.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no table and therefore no label column. Every quantity the paper reports (condensate size, fluorescence recovery half-time, DNA-bound cluster intensity, loops per chromatin domain) exists only as points plotted in a figure; to model anything you would have to re-derive the measurements from microscopy images that were never released.

a3_inputs_present.note: The model inputs would be the single-molecule fluorescence movies, atomic force microscopy images and super-resolution localisation lists. None are deposited; the supplementary movies are rendered video clips of selected fields, not the raw frames with calibration.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated clearly in the figure legends and methods (kilobases for loop sizes, micrometres for cluster size, seconds for recovery times) - but they describe figure axes, not any file.

a5_enough_rows.note: The biggest sample anywhere is 2,721 chromatin loops called by the authors from a public Micro-C dataset, and that is a derived annotation that was not released. The paper's own measurements are at the scale of 7-8 imaged cells and tens to a few hundred molecules per condition, far under the ~1,500-row bar.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Size is not the problem here; there is simply no quantitative dataset to load.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be checked at all, because no file exists against which to compare the paper's counts. This is the failure mode the checklist warns about, in its strongest form.

a8_label_provenance.note: The only label-like quantities with reasonable counts (loops per domain) are outputs of the authors' own unreleased dot-calling pipeline run on someone else's Micro-C contact maps, i.e. an algorithm's output rather than a direct measurement, and the pipeline parameters are only partly described.

backbone.name: none applicable
backbone.licence: Article is CC-BY 4.0, but no data object is released to license.

integration.partner_dataset: 4D Nucleome Micro-C (HFFc6, accession 4DNFI9FVHJZQ) and GEO GSE151553 yeast Micro-C, both public and reused by this paper
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could not be written for this paper's own data, because the paper contributes no joinable records - only the third-party contact maps are joinable, and they belong to other publications.

controls.positive_control: None definable without data; in principle the model would have to recover the known enrichment of chromatin loops between cohesin-bound sites.
controls.negative_control: Not runnable - no features or labels to shuffle.
controls.external_validation: The human HFFc6 Micro-C versus yeast Micro-C comparison would be a cross-species external test, but both are other groups' datasets, not this paper's.

honest_claim_h3: No honest modelling claim can be made from this paper, because it releases no measurements: any claim would rest on figure points re-digitised by eye or on third-party Micro-C data that this paper did not produce.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use microscopy images of protein-DNA assemblies to predict whether a chromosome-folding protein forms a droplet-like cluster.
plain_idea.train_on: The project considered would have trained on single-molecule fluorescence movies and atomic force microscopy images of four purified chromosome-maintenance protein complexes bound to DNA of varying length. The number of imaged molecules is unknown - the paper reports only 7-8 cells for the in-cell imaging and never gives a per-molecule count.
plain_idea.predict: Whether, and how strongly, a protein-DNA assembly condenses into a cluster, with the true answer coming from the authors' manual image analysis (regions of interest drawn in ImageJ, contours from OpenCV, fluorescence recovery curves).
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Chromosome-biology labs argue about whether loop extrusion alone explains genome folding, so an automated, quantitative read-out of protein-DNA condensation would make that argument testable across labs; but it needs released images, which this paper does not provide.

ml_idea: The only machine-learning idea this paper supports would be image-based: segment and classify DNA-bound protein condensates in single-molecule and atomic-force microscopy images, or predict multi-loop chromatin domains from contact maps. Neither is possible from this paper - the images are not deposited, and the contact maps belong to two earlier publications (4D Nucleome 4DNFI9FVHJZQ and GEO GSE151553) that would be the real data source. Chromatin-loop prediction from contact maps is in any case already served by several open deep-learning tools (DLoopCaller, DconnLoop, CGLoop, Mustache).

effort.compute_note: Not estimated: there is no dataset to size. The only retrievable object is a 55.6 MB supplementary zip of figures and movies, whose size I read from the PubMed Central XML rather than by downloading it.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the data availability statement and the supplementary file manifest - 'All data are available in the main text or the supplementary materials' plus a single figures-and-movies zip with zero supplementary tables kills the project in five minutes.

verdict_reason: A single-molecule biophysics paper that deposits no data. The data availability statement points only to the main text and supplementary materials, and the supplement is one 55.6 MB zip of ten figures and eight movies with no tables (verified in the PubMed Central full-text XML; the zip itself was not retrievable through Europe PMC or PubMed Central). Fails A1 (nothing to download), A2 (no label column - all measurements live as plotted points in figures), A3 (raw images not released), A5 (largest n is 2,721 loops derived from a third party's Micro-C; the paper's own imaging is 7-8 cells), A7 (no file exists to check counts against) and A8 (the loop labels are output of an unreleased dot-calling pipeline). The only downloadable data it touches, the public human and yeast Micro-C contact maps, belong to earlier papers and are already a crowded machine-learning target.
